Explain the historical development of quantum mechanics, including the experiments that led to the concept of wave-particle duality. 5. Perform measurements and analyze results in laboratory experiments using concepts from this course.
designations: Core GenEd - Natural Science & Wellness + Lab Breadth - Physical Science Level - Intermediate L&S Credit - L&S Liberal Arts and Science

courses.title: A Modern Introduction to Physics
courses.description: Continuation of PHYSICS 248 . Modern physics: introduction to quantum mechanics, topics from nuclear and particle physics, condensed matter physics, and atomic physics. Three lectures and one discussion per week.
courses.requisitesRaw: PHYSICS 248
learningOutcomes: 1. Determine time-dependent voltage changes across components and flow of alternating electric currents through circuits. Describe the foundations of modern electronics. 2. Determine statistical properties of gases using the ideal gas law and principles of heat transfer. Calculate changes in work, heat, entropy, and energy resulting from thermodynamic processes. 3. Explain the foundational concepts from modern fields of physics such as atomic physics, solid state physics, nuclear physics, particle physics, condensed matter physics, and astrophysics. Perform elementary calculations related to these fields. 4. Apply computational skills that are commonly used in physics research.
designations: Core GenEd - Natural Science & Wellness + Lab Breadth - Physical Science Level - Intermediate L&S Credit - L&S Liberal Arts and Science

courses.title: Mechanics
courses.description: Origin and development of classical mechanics; mathematical techniques, especially vector analysis; conservation laws and their relation to symmetry principles; brief introduction to orbit theory and rigid-body dynamics; accelerated coordinate systems; introduction to the generalized-coordinate formalisms of Lagrange and Hamilton.
courses.requisitesRaw: ( PHYSICS 202 , 208 , or 248 ) and ( MATH 234 , 321 , or 376 ), or graduate/professional standing
learningOutcomes: 1. Use Newton's laws of motion to solve advanced problems involving the dynamic motion of classical mechanical systems. 2. Apply differential equations and other advanced mathematics to solve dynamic motion of classical mechanical systems. 3. Analyze and solve dynamics problems using conservation of energy and linear and angular momentum. 4. Calculate properties and behaviors of rigid body motion and motion of continuous media. 5. Derive the equations of motion for complicated mechanical systems using the Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations of classical mechanics. 6. Apply the Lagrangian formulation to analyze the motion of constrained systems.
designations: Core GenEd - Natural Science & Wellness + Lab Breadth - Physical Science Level - Advanced L&S Credit - L&S Liberal Arts and Science

courses.title: Electromagnetic Fields
courses.description: Electrostatic fields, capacitance, multi-pole expansion, dielectric theory; magnetostatics; electromagnetic induction; magnetic properties of matter; Maxwell's equations and electromagnetic waves; relativity and electromagnetism.
courses.requisitesRaw: ( PHYSICS 202 , 208 or 248 ) and ( MATH 234 , 321 or 376 ), or graduate/professional standing
learningOutcomes: 1. Calculate the electric field, electric potential, and total energy directly from charge distributions. 2. Calculate the static properties of currents, magnetic fields, and magnetic vector potentials. 3. Apply vector algebra and vector calculus to calculate electric and magnetic fields. 4. Calculate electric potential distributions using Laplace's equation, and apply method of images, separation of variables, and multipole expansions. 5. Calculate the static electromagnetic response of continuous media. 6. Calculate properties of electric and magnetic fields changing in time. 7. Use Maxwell's equations to calculate the properties of electromagnetic waves.
designations: Core GenEd - Natural Science & Wellness + Lab Breadth - Physical Science Level - Advanced L&S Credit - L&S Liberal Arts and Science

courses.title: Atomic and Quantum Physics
courses.description: Review of atomic and other quantum phenomena and special relativity; introduction to quantum mechanics treating the more advanced topics of atomic physics and applications to molecular, solid state, nuclear, and elementary particle physics and quantum statistics.
courses.requisitesRaw: ( PHYSICS 205 , 241 , 249 , or PHYSICS/E C E 235 ) and PHYSICS 311 and 322 , or graduate/professional standing
designations: Core GenEd - Natural Science & Wellness Breadth - Physical Science Level - Advanced L&S Credit - L&S Liberal Arts and Science

courses.title: Introduction to Quantum Mechanics
courses.description: Historical background and experimental basis of quantum mechanics; de Broglie waves, correspondence principle, uncertainty principle, Schrodinger equation, hydrogen atom, electron spin, Pauli principle; applications of wave mechanics.
courses.requisitesRaw: ( PHYSICS 205 , 241 , 249 , or PHYSICS/E C E 235 ) and PHYSICS 311 and 322 , or graduate/professional standing
learningOutcomes: 1. Master the concept of the wavefunction Audience: Both Grad & Undergrad 2. Perform statistical analysis using operator algebra 3. Understand the energy levels of the hydrogen atom Audience: Both Grad & Undergrad 4. Obtain the mathematical skills necessary to solve the 3-dimensional wave equation 5. Acquire the skills necessary to apply various types of perturbation theory Audience: Both Grad & Undergrad 6. Use the variational principle including taking advantage of symmetry 7. Understand the necessary mathematical apparatus of scattering theory Audience: Both Grad & Undergrad 8. Discuss and explain fully the logical foundations of quantum mechanics Audience: Both Grad & Undergrad
designations: Core GenEd - Natural Science & Wellness Breadth - Physical Science Level - Advanced L&S Credit - L&S Liberal Arts and Science Grad 50% - Counts toward 50% graduate coursework requirement

courses.title: Solid State Physics
courses.description: Mechanical, thermal, electric, and magnetic properties of solids; band theory; semiconductors; crystal imperfections.
courses.requisitesRaw: PHYSICS 205 , 241 , 249 , 448 , 531 , PHYSICS/E C E 235 , or graduate/professional standing
learningOutcomes: 1. Utilize ideas of atomic bonding to understand crystal lattice structures and reciprocal space Audience: Both Grad & Undergrad 2. Use the reciprocal lattice to determine complex x-ray diffraction patterns 3. Become familiar with the calculation of simple phonon dispersion relations and use them to determine lattice thermal properties Audience: Both Grad & Undergrad 4. Master the electronic properties of metals in the quantum free-electron model and distinguish insulators, metals, and semiconductors Audience: Both Grad & Undergrad 5. Obtain the ability to calculate general band structures in the nearly-free electronic and tight-binding approximations 6. Analyze and calculate properties of bulk semiconductors and semiconductor junctions Audience: Both Grad & Undergrad 7. Describe quantitatively ordered systems such as ferroelectrics, ferromagnets and superconductors Audience: Both Grad & Undergrad 8. Understand the physics of superconducting junctions
designations: Core GenEd - Natural Science & Wellness Breadth - Physical Science Level - Advanced L&S Credit - L&S Liberal Arts and Science Grad 50% - Counts toward 50% graduate coursework requirement

courses.title: Data Science Modeling I
courses.description: Introduces reproducible data management, modeling, analysis, and statistical inference through a practical, hands-on case studies approach. Topics include the use of an integrated statistical computing environment, data wrangling, the R programming language, data graphics and visualization, random variables and concepts of probability including the binomial and normal distributions, data modeling, statistical inference in one- and two- sample settings for proportions and means, simple linear regression, and report generation using R Markdown with applications to a wide variety of data to address open-ended questions.
courses.requisitesRaw: Satisfied Quantitative Reasoning (QR) A
learningOutcomes: 1. wrangle data: transform data, possibly from multiple sources, into a form convenient for analysis 2. explore data: visualize and summarize data, generate questions/hypotheses, and address them 3. program: write R code using the R Studio integrated statistical computing environment to carry out reproducible data analysis 4. model data: use probability and random variables in statistical computing environment to carry out reproducible data analysis 5. interpret data: explain what can be inferred from the data analysis and make predictions 6. communicate: use R Markdown to integrate prose, visualizations, code, interpretation, and results 7. collaborate: work with other students to solve data challenges 8. make statistical inferences: employ confidence intervals and hypothesis tests using both computational and standard methods such as binomial and t-tests
designations: Core GenEd - Mathematics & Quantitative Reasoning Comm QR - Quantitative Reasoning B Breadth - Natural Science Level - Intermediate L&S Credit - L&S Liberal Arts and Science

courses.title: Introduction to Statistical Methods
courses.description: Distributions, measures of central tendency, dispersion and shape, the normal distribution; experiments to compare means, standard errors, confidence intervals; effects of departure from assumption; method of least squares, regression, correlation, assumptions and limitations; basic ideas of experimental design.
courses.requisitesRaw: Satisfied Quantitative Reasoning (QR) A. Not open to students with credit for STAT 302, 324 , or 371 .
courses.exclusionsRaw: Not open to students with credit for STAT 302, STAT 324 , or STAT 371 .
learningOutcomes: 1. Describe statistics as a discipline and why statistics can be useful for furthering scientific research 2. Demonstrate a general understanding of the core concepts of statistics, including probability, sampling distributions, estimation, confidence intervals, and hypothesis testing 3. Create useful graphs and summaries of data, and perform basic statistical analyses when appropriate, including one- and two-sample and paired tests for means, chi-squared tests, correlations, and simple linear regressions 4. Correctly interpret statistical graphs and results in terms of the original scientific context in which the data was gathered, and identify common pitfalls that lead to compromised or misleading results 5. Recognize when to seek statistical help and have a sufficient understanding of statistical terminology to communicate meaningfully with a professional statistician
designations: Core GenEd - Mathematics & Quantitative Reasoning Comm QR - Quantitative Reasoning B Breadth - Natural Science Level - Intermediate L&S Credit - L&S Liberal Arts and Science

courses.title: R for Statistics I
courses.description: An understanding of the commonly used statistical language R. Topics will include using R to manipulate data and perform exploratory data analysis.
courses.requisitesRaw: STAT 240 , 301 , 302, 312 , 324 , 371 , MATH/STAT 310 , ECON 310 , GEN BUS 303, 304, 306 , 307 , 317 , PSYCH 210 , B M E 325 , I SY E 210 , SOC/C&E SOC 360 , POLI SCI 270 , graduate/professional standing, or declared in Statistics VISP
learningOutcomes: 1. Use basic R vocabulary 2. Manipulate data in R 3. Produce graphics and reports 4. Apply statistical methods 5. Run basic simulations
designations: Core GenEd - Natural Science & Wellness Breadth - Natural Science Level - Intermediate L&S Credit - L&S Liberal Arts and Science

courses.title: Introduction to Probability and Mathematical Statistics I
courses.description: Probability and combinatorial methods, discrete and continuous, univariate and multivariate distributions, expected values, moments, normal distribution and derived distributions, estimation.
courses.requisitesRaw: MATH 234 , 376 , or concurrent enrollment. Not open to students with credit for STAT/MATH 431 or STAT 311
courses.exclusionsRaw: Not open to students with credit for STAT 431 or STAT 311
learningOutcomes: 1. Recall the definitions of fundamental objects and concepts underlying probability theory (e.g. sample spaces and events, the axioms of probability, the notions of conditional probability and independence, random variables and their probability distributions, mathematical expectation, and the joint distribution of one or more random variables) and demonstrate understanding of their properties 2. Perform important operations in probability (e.g. calculate the probabilities of events, derive the probability distributions of random variables, compute moments and the expectation of functions of random variables, calculate covariances and correlations, and obtain conditional distributions and conditional expectations) and interpret the results 3. Explain the meaning of key results in probability theory that are especially important in mathematical statistics (e.g. Bayes’ Theorem, probabilistic tail inequalities such as Markov’s and Chebyshev’s inequalities, the Law of Large Numbers, and the Central Limit Theorem) 4. Identify, utilize, and understand the key properties of, probability distributions that are especially important in statistics, including discrete families of distributions (e.g. the binomial, Poisson, geometric, and negative binomial distributions) and continuous families of distributions (e.g. the uniform, exponential, gamma, and normal distributions)
designations: Core GenEd - Natural Science & Wellness Breadth - Natural Science Level - Advanced L&S Credit - L&S Liberal Arts and Science

courses.title: Introduction to Theory and Methods of Mathematical Statistics I
courses.description: Elements of probability, important discrete distributions, acceptance sampling by attributes, sample characteristics, probability distributions and population characteristics, the normal distribution, acceptance sampling plans based on sample means and variances, sampling from the normal, the central limit theorem, point and interval estimation.
courses.requisitesRaw: MATH 234 , 376 , or concurrent enrollment or graduate/professsional standing. Not open to students with credit for STAT/MATH 309 or STAT/MATH 431
courses.exclusionsRaw: Not open to students with credit for STAT 309 or STAT 431
designations: Core GenEd - Natural Science & Wellness Breadth - Natural Science Level - Advanced L&S Credit - L&S Liberal Arts and Science

courses.title: Introduction to Theory and Methods of Mathematical Statistics II
courses.description: Unbiased estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, confidence intervals, tests of hypotheses, Neyman-Pearson lemma, likelihood ratio test, regression, analysis of variance with applications.
courses.requisitesRaw: STAT/MATH 309 , STAT 311 , STAT/MATH 431 , MATH 531 , or graduate/professional standing
learningOutcomes: 1. Be able to use probability theory to understand and utilize three principal tools of statistical inference: point estimators, confidence intervals, and hypothesis tests. 2. Understand and be able to use standard statistical procedures for analyzing numerical data in certain contexts. These include inference for the mean based on a single random sample; comparing two means based on two random samples; Analysis of Variance; simple linear regression. 3. Understand and be able to use standard statistical procedures for analyzing binary and categorical data in certain contexts. These include one- and two-sample inference for proportions, and the analysis of one- and two-way contingency tables for multi-category data. 4. Identify the assumptions behind statistical procedures and understand their importance. Be able to recognize when techniques based on standard reference distributions (normal, chi-square, T- and F-distribution) are valid or not, and be able to utilize certain alternatives such as exact or nonparametric methods when they are required or preferable.
designations: Core GenEd - Natural Science & Wellness Breadth - Natural Science Level - Advanced L&S Credit - L&S Liberal Arts and Science

courses.title: Introduction to Statistics for Science and Engineering
courses.description: Descriptive statistics, probability concepts and distributions, random variables. Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals for one- and two-sample problems. Linear regression, model checking, and inference. Analysis of variance and basic ideas in experimental design. Utilizes the R programming language.
courses.requisitesRaw: MATH 211 , 217, or 221 . Not open to students with credit for STAT 371 .
courses.exclusionsRaw: Not open to students with credit for STAT 371 .
learningOutcomes: 1. Articulate the basics of probability and statistics. 2. Make numeric and graphical summaries of simple data 3. Produce appropriate statistical analyses of simple data sets 4. Design simple experiments with data that will suit basic statistical analysis 5. Use R for statistical computations and graphs 6. Learn additional statistical methods
designations: Core GenEd - Mathematics & Quantitative Reasoning Level - Intermediate L&S Credit - L&S Liberal Arts and Science

courses.title: Applied Regression Analysis
courses.description: A foundational understanding of linear regression and how it is used for prediction, feature selection and interpretation. In particular, the impact of correlated/dependent features and the role and violation of key assumptions are studied. Extensions such as mixed models and generalized linear models are also discussed. Utilizes the R programming language.
courses.requisitesRaw: ( STAT 240 , 301 , 302, 312 , 324 , 371 , ECON 310 , B M E 325 , GEN BUS 306 , I SY E 210 , or POLI SCI 270 ) and (STAT 327 or 303 , or concurrent enrollment)
learningOutcomes: 1. Correctly choose and apply common regression methods that are used in practice to analyze data, including simple and multiple linear regressions, ANOVAs/ANCOVAs, generalized linear models (e.g. logistic and Poisson) and fixed/random/mixed effect models 2. Identify the underlying assumptions behind common regression methods and utilize diagnostic tools to detect violations of said assumptions 3. Correctly interpret and explain results from regression methods, including interpretation of the coefficients, the p-values, R-squared, and other statistical summaries from regression 4. Apply these methods to real data using the free statistical software R
designations: Core GenEd - Natural Science & Wellness + Lab Breadth - Natural Science Level - Advanced L&S Credit - L&S Liberal Arts and Science

courses.title: Data Science Modeling II
courses.description: Teaches how to explore, model, and analyze data using R. Topics include basic probability models; the central limit theorem; Monte Carlo simulation; one- and two-sample hypothesis testing; Bayesian inference; linear and logistic regression; ANOVA; the bootstrap; random forests and cross-validation. Features the analysis of real-world data sets and the communication of findings in a clear and reproducible manner within a project setting.
courses.requisitesRaw: ( MATH 211 , 217, or 221 ) and STAT 240
learningOutcomes: 1. Understand and apply basic concepts in probability; combine basic probability models to build more complicated ones; and critique models and their assumptions 2. Formulate statistical hypotheses for different kinds of research questions and test those hypotheses using both classical and Monte Carlo methods. 3. Understand and apply principles of statistical estimation and prediction, including fitting models and assessing model quality, in the context of both linear and logistic regression. 4. Apply statistical tools to answer research questions using real-world data and present these findings clearly in both spoken and written form to non-experts.
designations: Core GenEd - Natural Science & Wellness + Lab Breadth - Natural Science Level - Intermediate L&S Credit - L&S Liberal Arts and Science

courses.title: Introductory Applied Statistics for the Life Sciences
courses.description: Introduction to modern statistical practice in the life sciences, using the R programming language. Topics include: exploratory data analysis, probability and random variables; one-sample testing and confidence intervals, role of assumptions, sample size determination, two-sample inference; basic ideas in experimental design, analysis of variance, linear regression, goodness-of fit; biological applications.
courses.requisitesRaw: ( MATH 112 and placed out of MATH 113 ), ( MATH 113 and placed out of MATH 112 ), ( MATH 112 and 113 ), MATH 114 , 171, 211 , 221 , or placement in MATH 221 . Not open to students with credit for STAT 302 or 324
courses.exclusionsRaw: Not open to students with credit for STAT 302 or STAT 324
learningOutcomes: 1. Articulate the basics of probability and statistics 2. Make numeric and graphical summaries of simple data 3. Produce appropriate statistical analyses of simple data sets 4. Design simple experiments whose data will suit basic statistical analysis 5. Use RStudio, a free statistical software package, for statistical computations and graphs 6. Study and learn additional statistical methods
designations: Core GenEd - Mathematics & Quantitative Reasoning Comm QR - Quantitative Reasoning B Breadth - Natural Science Level - Intermediate L&S Credit - L&S Liberal Arts and Science

courses.title: Applied Categorical Data Analysis
courses.description: "Which is more popular, Apple, PC, or Linux?" "Rate your satisfaction with this product on a scale from 1 to 5." Organizing information into categories is natural! But, canonical statistical approaches like standard linear regression are not designed for analyzing such data. Develop techniques appropriate for analyzing categorical response data, with an emphasis on their application. Topics include: multidimensional contingency tables, inference for measures of association between categorical variables, and regression modeling for categorical data - specifically, logistic & Poisson regression. Utilizes the R programming language.
courses.requisitesRaw: STAT 333 , 340 , graduate/professional standing, or declared in Statistics VISP
learningOutcomes: 1. Construct and interpret contingency tables for the purposes of summarizing, displaying, exploring, and analyzing data classified by one or more categorical variables. 2. Calculate and interpret summary measures of association between categorical variables, such as odds ratios. 3. Perform inference for parameters of interest arising from models of categorical data by using point estimators, confidence intervals, and hypothesis tests, and interpreting their results. 4. Fit logistic and Poisson regression models where appropriate; assess the goodness of the model fits; perform model selection; and interpret/make inferences from well-fitting models. This includes the important subcases of fitting logistic and loglinear models to contingency tables. 5. Utilize a statistical computing package (such as R) to carry out analyses of categorical data.
designations: Core GenEd - Natural Science & Wellness Breadth - Natural Science Level - Advanced L&S Credit - L&S Liberal Arts and Science

courses.title: Statistical Experimental Design
courses.description: Introduction to statistical design and analysis of experiments. Topics include: principles of randomization, blocking and replication, randomized blocking designs, Latin square designs, full factorial and fractional factorial designs and response surface methodology. Substantial focus will be devoted to engineering applications. A brief review on using design of experiments for digital transformation and A/B testing will be provided.
courses.requisitesRaw: ( MATH/STAT 310 , STAT 333 , or 340 ) or (declared in Mechanical Engineering BS and one of STAT 240 , 301 , 302, 312 , 324 , 371 , or I SY E 210 ), or graduate/professional standing
nonCourseReqs: declared in Mechanical Engineering BS and one of STAT 240
learningOutcomes: 1. Describe key concepts in the design and analysis of experiments. 2. Generate experimental designs and apply appropriate analysis techniques. 3. Compare different experimental design and analysis methods in various scenarios. 4. Apply experimental design and analysis methods in real-world projects. 5. Implement experimental design and analysis methods in statistical software like R.
designations: Core GenEd - Natural Science & Wellness + Lab Breadth - Natural Science Level - Advanced L&S Credit - L&S Liberal Arts and Science

courses.title: Applied Multivariate Analysis
courses.description: Multivariate statistical learning methods are essential and broadly applicable tools for analyzing and understanding complex datasets. Emphasizes the conceptual underpinnings, core models, and basic statistical reasoning underlying the techniques. Topics include: dimension reduction (e.g., principal component analysis, multidimensional scaling, factor analysis), clustering (e.g., k-means, hierarchical, density-based, and model-based clustering), and classification (e.g., discriminant analysis, classification tree, and ensemble methods). Utilizes the R programming language.
courses.requisitesRaw: ( STAT 333 or 340 ) and ( MATH 320 , 340 , 341 , 345 , or 375 ), graduate/professional standing, or declared in Statistics VISP
learningOutcomes: 1. Describe the purpose and basic concepts of multivariate analysis, distinguishing it from other common forms of statistical analysis such as regression analysis. 2. Define fundamental concepts of multivariate analysis, such as covariance and correlation, and explain their meaning. 3. Explain common methods of multivariate analysis such as principal components analysis, factor analysis, multidimensional scaling, and clustering; this includes identifying situations in which these methods would be useful, describing how they are performed, and explaining how to interpret their outputs. 4. Use statistical software such as R to create meaningful visualizations of multivariate data, and to carry out multivariate analyses. 5. Properly interpret, contextualize, and communicate the results of an applied multivariate analysis.
designations: Core GenEd - Natural Science & Wellness Breadth - Natural Science Level - Advanced L&S Credit - L&S Liberal Arts and Science

courses.title: Financial Statistics
courses.description: Today's cutting-edge quantitative trading strategies are based on complex stochastic models of financial data. Specialized statistical techniques are needed to analyze them. Study the advanced statistical methodologies now widely employed in modern finance. Topics include: discrete models such as binomial trees and GARCH; continuous models such as the Black-Scholes model; and stochastic volatility models. Emphasis will be on data analysis and statistical inference in these models, with applications to risk management. Learn about the models real quantitative traders use in their work.
courses.requisitesRaw: ( STAT 333 , 340 , or ECON 410 ) and ( MATH/STAT 309 , STAT 311 , MATH 331 , MATH/STAT 431 , or MATH 531 ), graduate/professional standing, or declared in Statistics VISP
learningOutcomes: 1. Describe basic stochastic models used in pricing financial instruments. 2. Develop statistical inferences for financial applications to volatility analysis and risk management. 3. Use computer packages to perform statistical analysis of financial data. 4. Interpret statistical analysis in the context of financial applications
designations: Core GenEd - Natural Science & Wellness Level - Advanced L&S Credit - L&S Liberal Arts and Science

courses.title: Introduction to Combinatorics
courses.description: Problems of enumeration, distribution, and arrangement. Inclusion-exclusion principle. Generating functions and linear recurrence relations. Combinatorial identities. Graph coloring problems. Finite designs. Systems of distinct representatives and matching problems in graphs. Potential applications in the social, biological, and physical sciences. Puzzles. Problem solving.
courses.requisitesRaw: ( MATH 320 , 340 , 341 , 345 , or 375 ), graduate/professional standing, or declared in Mathematics VISP (undergraduate or graduate)
learningOutcomes: 1. Understand basic counting strategies, such as staged thought-experiments, inclusion/exclusion, generating functions, and recurrence relations, and apply these strategies to solve a wide variety of counting problems. 2. Recall basic objects that are used in combinatorics, such as permutations and combinations of sets and multisets, binomial and multinomial coefficients, the Catalan numbers, the Stirling numbers, and the partition numbers. 3. Analyze a given combinatorial problem using the standard theorems of combinatorics, such as the pigeonhole principle, the Newton binomial theorem, the multinomial theorem, the Ramsey theorem, the Dilworth theorem, the Burnside theorem, and the Polya counting theorem. 4. Construct mathematical arguments related to combinatorial problems using the above definitions, properties, theorems, and counting strategies; including the construction of examples and counterexamples. 5. Convey arguments in oral and written form in English, using appropriate mathematical terminology, notation, and grammar.
designations: Core GenEd - Natural Science & Wellness Breadth - Natural Science Level - Advanced L&S Credit - L&S Liberal Arts and Science

courses.title: Introduction to Biostatistics
courses.description: Course designed for the biomedical researcher. Topics include: descriptive statistics, hypothesis testing, estimation, confidence intervals, t-tests, chi-squared tests, analysis of variance, linear regression, correlation, nonparametric tests, survival analysis and odds ratio. Biomedical applications used for each topic.
courses.requisitesRaw: Graduate/professional standing. Not open to students with credit for STAT 511 or POP HLTH/B M I 551
courses.exclusionsRaw: Not open to students with credit for STAT 511 or POP HLTH 551
learningOutcomes: 1. Understand building blocks and fundamentals that support core themes of Biostatistics in the application of biomedicine and public health Audience: Both Grad & Undergrad 2. Conduct basic statistical analyses of biomedical data Audience: Both Grad & Undergrad 3. Use R for statistical computing Audience: Both Grad & Undergrad 4. Critique methods and evidence from others' studies 5. Collaborate effectively with biostatisticians
designations: Level - Intermediate L&S Credit - L&S Liberal Arts and Science Grad 50% - Counts toward 50% graduate coursework requirement

courses.title: Statistical Methods for Bioscience I
courses.description: Descriptive statistics, distributions, one- and two-sample normal inference, power, one-way ANOVA, simple linear regression, categorical data, non-parametric methods; underlying assumptions and diagnostic work.
courses.requisitesRaw: Graduate/professional standing
designations: Level - Intermediate L&S Credit - L&S Liberal Arts and Science Grad 50% - Counts toward 50% graduate coursework requirement
